ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Gauging | Orlando, FL UT
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and weld UT in Orlando, FL for chilled-water and steam piping, tanks, attraction steel and plant equipment. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Inspection in Orlando, Florida
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in Orlando, Florida: wall-thickness surveys on corroded piping, tanks and vessels, and angle-beam examination of structural and pressure welds in carbon steel. The work suits central-Florida owners whose assets run in heat and humidity, from resort and convention energy plants to utility and fuel facilities, attraction structures and fabrication shops. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Send your equipment list through the UT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Orlando

Orlando is not a refinery town, and that shapes the work. The region is built on tourism, hospitality, aviation, defense electronics and simulation, and fast-growing construction, and each of those depends on steel that must keep carrying load or pressure. A great deal of that steel is hidden behind ceilings, in mechanical rooms, under rides or inside storage tanks, so thickness readings and weld examinations are often the first real look an owner gets.

  • Resort, hotel and convention energy plants: chilled-water and condenser-water piping, steam and hot-water lines, boiler shells, deaerators, expansion tanks and the headers that serve very large air-conditioned buildings year round.
  • Attractions and entertainment structure: support towers, track and frame welds, lift structure and pressure components, where owners and engineers want proof of sound metal beyond a visual look.
  • Airport and fuel facilities: atmospheric storage tanks, hydrant and transfer piping and the supports around the airport district.
  • Utility and water systems: gas-fired generating plants in Orange County, steam and feedwater piping, cooling-tower basins, and the wastewater and water-treatment steel serving a metro of millions.
  • Construction and fabrication: structural steel for towers, parking structures and stadium-type buildings, plus the welds in shops supplying the region's growth.

The shared theme is steel that sits in humid air and warm water all year, so corrosion under insulation and on the inside of water piping is a standing concern.

What ultrasonic testing finds and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing launches a high-frequency pulse into the steel and times the return echo from the far wall or from a flaw. Since the velocity of sound in steel is known, the instrument converts time into distance, which makes UT the standard method for measuring thickness from one side and for examining the volume of a weld without cutting it.

  • It finds: uniform wall loss, localized pitting under a probe, laminations, erosion at bends and tees, and weld flaws such as lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, cracks and slag.
  • It can miss: shallow cracks hidden in the near-surface dead zone, flaws lying parallel to the beam, and defects in coarse-grained material or under thick, poorly bonded coatings.
  • It requires: access to one side of the component, a smooth enough surface, couplant, calibration on a block of the right material, and a technician who can read the A-scan rather than trusting a number alone.

For surface cracks in carbon steel welds, magnetic particle testing in Orlando is the better search tool, and for cracks in stainless steel penetrant testing fits.

Thickness surveys on piping and tanks

Most Orlando ultrasonic work is corrosion mapping. The owner or the engineer defines condition monitoring locations on piping, vessels and tank shells, and the technician returns to the same points each cycle. This is the practice behind API 570 piping programs, API 510 vessel programs, API 653 tank programs, and the maintenance plans of energy plants that are not under those codes at all.

  1. Mark the locations and clean each reading area to bare, sound metal as far as the owner allows.
  2. Calibrate a dual-element probe on a step block of the same alloy, and confirm the zero and velocity at the temperature of the work.
  3. Take readings while watching the A-scan, which exposes double echoes on thin wall and the sudden drop of a pit.
  4. Record the lowest reading at each point, mark the piping isometric or tank drawing, and compare with nominal and required minimum thickness.

Chilled-water piping often sweats, so the outside of the pipe may be wet and under insulation; the owner removes insulation at the survey points and the technician makes sure the area is dry enough for couplant to couple properly. Thickness practice follows ASTM E797 and the Section V thickness requirements.

Weld examination with angle-beam probes

For groove welds in plate and pipe, technicians use shear-wave angle-beam probes, usually 45, 60 or 70 degrees, on a reference curve built from side-drilled holes. They scan from both sides where access allows, scan the whole weld and heat-affected zone, and evaluate indications against the recording and rejection levels in the governing code. In central Florida this often means welds in structural steel, repaired pressure vessel seams and piping welds in energy plants, and examinations after fabrication or repair.

The code decides whether UT may be used for the job, which indications are rejectable and how the report must be organized. We work from the code and edition on your contract rather than from habit.

Codes and Florida's own regime

  • ASME Section V: Article 4 for weld examination, Article 5 for materials and Article 23 for thickness practice.
  • AWS D1.1: steel structures, with ultrasonic examination of groove welds and its own acceptance tables; AWS D1.5 governs steel bridge welding where Florida DOT work is involved.
  • ASME B31.3 and B31.1: process and power piping examination and acceptance.
  • ASME Section VIII Division 1: Appendix 12 for UT of pressure vessel welds.
  • API 510, 570 and 653: in-service inspection codes; the owner's authorized inspector is responsible, and Atlantis supplies the examination data.

Florida adds its own layer. The Boiler Safety Section of the Bureau of Fire Prevention, in the Division of State Fire Marshal, administers the Boiler Safety Act, Chapter 554 of the Florida Statutes, and Rule 69A-51 of the Florida Administrative Code, with deputy boiler inspectors assigned by region including central Florida. Amusement rides fall under the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, whose Bureau of Fair Rides Inspection requires non-destructive testing for metal fatigue on many rides at least annually, by a technician who meets the standards in the department's rule. Confirm the requirement for your equipment with the agency before you book, because who may perform the testing is set by rule, not by us.

Who does the work in Orlando

Atlantis has no office in Orlando. Technicians are mobilized to your property, plant or shop for the agreed scope. They are qualified under Atlantis's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, so that a Level II performs and interprets the examination while an ASNT Level III approves the procedures and reviews the reports. Anoop Rayavarapu, the founder, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. The company is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Procedures are written to the code on your contract, so acceptance criteria are fixed before the first reading.

What the ultrasonic report contains

  • Equipment tag or line number, material, nominal and minimum required thickness, and location.
  • Procedure and revision, code and edition, and the acceptance criteria applied.
  • Instrument, probe and calibration block identification, with calibration checks recorded.
  • Technician name and level, date, and surface temperature at the time of the examination.
  • Thickness grids or point tables with the lowest value flagged; for welds, indication position, length, amplitude, depth and accept or reject.
  • Marked-up drawings or isometrics so that the next survey is repeatable.

Your engineer or authorized inspector can follow any result to a calibrated reading without a follow-up call.

Planning an ultrasonic job in Orlando

  • Afternoon thunderstorms: summer storms arrive on a near-daily rhythm, and lightning stops outdoor work on roofs, towers and tanks, so critical outdoor readings are planned for mornings.
  • Heat and humidity: hot roofs and equipment pads affect people and probes, and condensation on cold chilled-water lines affects couplant.
  • Hurricane season: June through November can interrupt schedules and demand quick condition checks after a storm.
  • Guest areas: at resorts, attractions and airports, work in or near public spaces is usually scheduled around operating hours, with strict escort, badge and safety rules.
  • Insulation and access: removal of insulation, scaffolding and lift access all affect the cost of the visit, so settle them in the scope.

Tell us your drawings, access method and the dates your equipment is out of service, and we plan mobilization around them without promising a crew arrival time.

Choosing between UT, MT and PT in Orlando

Use ultrasonic testing for remaining wall and for the inside of welds. Use magnetic particle inspection for surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, for example at lifting lugs and structural welds. Use liquid penetrant testing for surface cracks in stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic metal. Florida's statewide inspection services hub gathers all three, and the UT service overview and UT guide explain the method in more depth.

Training your own ultrasonic technicians

Facilities teams that read thickness every season often prefer a trained person on staff. Atlantis teaches UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 under SNT-TC-1A, supported by the UT practical simulator. Your company certifies its technicians through its own written practice; see NDT training for Orlando employers and use the eligibility checker to see where a candidate stands.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic thickness testing cover in Orlando facilities?
faq.a: It measures remaining wall on piping, tanks, vessels and structure by timing a sound echo through the steel. In Orlando that includes chilled-water and steam piping, fuel storage, utility lines and attraction or building steel.

faq.q: Can Atlantis perform UT on welds as well as thickness gauging?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians use calibrated angle-beam probes, a reference curve and a full-volume scan, then judge indications against the construction code named on your contract, such as AWS D1.1 or ASME Section V.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Orlando?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Orlando. Technicians are mobilized to your property, plant or shop for the agreed scope and provide a written report with calibration records and thickness data.

faq.q: Can UT be done on chilled-water pipe that sweats?
faq.a: Yes, once the insulation is removed at the survey points and the surface is cleaned and dried enough for couplant to couple. Planning for insulation removal and moisture belongs in the scope of work.

faq.q: Which Florida agency oversees boilers?
faq.a: The Boiler Safety Section within the Bureau of Fire Prevention, Division of State Fire Marshal, administers Chapter 554 of the Florida Statutes and Rule 69A-51. Atlantis supplies NDE data and does not replace those inspections.

faq.q: Does Florida require nondestructive testing on amusement rides?
faq.a: Florida law requires non-destructive testing for metal fatigue on many rides at least annually, performed by a technician meeting the department's rule. Confirm eligibility with the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services before booking.

faq.q: Who is responsible for API 510, 570 or 653 inspection when Atlantis does the ultrasonic work?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection and the fitness decision. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and thickness survey and delivers documented data for that inspector.

faq.q: When should I choose MT or PT instead of UT in Orlando?
faq.a: Choose magnetic particle testing for surface cracks in carbon steel and penetrant testing for surface cracks in stainless or aluminum. Choose UT when the concern is wall loss or flaws inside a weld.

faq.q: Can my team learn UT through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis teaches UT Level 1 and Level 2 under ASNT SNT-TC-1A recommended practice, and your company then qualifies and certifies its technicians through its own written practice.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Orlando, FL | MPI & MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Orlando, FL for attraction steel, lifting gear, structural welds and plant equipment, mobilized to your site. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Orlando, Florida
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides magnetic particle inspection (MPI, or mag particle testing) in Orlando, Florida, to find surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel. Typical work includes welds on attraction and entertainment structures, lifting lugs and rigging, structural steel for towers and venues, and equipment at energy plants. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Send a list of the welds and parts through the MT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Orlando

Orlando's economy runs on structures that carry people, from rides and stage rigging to convention halls, towers and parking decks, and on the plants that keep those buildings cool and powered. Wherever welded carbon steel is stressed again and again, fatigue cracks start at the surface, and that is exactly what magnetic particle inspection is built to find.

  • Attraction and entertainment steel: weld toes on frames, supports and track structure, stage and theatrical rigging points, lifting lugs and pins. Florida's amusement ride rules call for periodic metal-fatigue testing on many rides, and magnetic particle inspection is a common surface method when the owner's engineer specifies it.
  • Buildings and towers: structural connections, crane-supported lifts during construction, anchor and bracket welds, and repairs after storm damage.
  • Energy and utility plants: nozzle and support welds on carbon steel vessels, lifting attachments on turbines and pumps, and hanger and support welds on piping.
  • Airport and ground equipment: fuel-handling frames, loading equipment, jacks and fabricated stands around the airport district.
  • Fabrication and construction shops: fillet and groove welds on beams, plates and weldments shipped to central Florida job sites.

Nearly all of this is ferromagnetic steel, the material on which magnetic particle inspection performs best.

What magnetic particle inspection finds and what it misses

Magnetizing a steel part creates a field inside it. A crack at or just under the surface interrupts that field and makes it leak out, and fine ferrous particles collect at the leak to draw the shape of the flaw. The result is a direct visual picture of the crack, within seconds of applying particles.

  • It finds: fatigue cracks, weld toe cracks, hot cracks, laps, seams and slight subsurface flaws in ferromagnetic steels, down to widths too narrow to see unaided.
  • It misses: flaws in austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, brass and other non-magnetic metals, and defects buried deep inside a section.
  • It prefers crossing cracks: flaws parallel to the field are weakly shown, so each area is examined twice with the field turned roughly ninety degrees.
  • It is affected by finish: thick coatings, heavy scale and rough weld surfaces reduce sensitivity and may need to be removed locally.

Where metal is non-magnetic or the area cannot be magnetized, penetrant testing in Orlando is the usual alternative, and where wall thickness is the question, ultrasonic testing is used.

Techniques used in the field

For work on structures and rides, the portable yoke is the standard tool. Its adjustable legs magnetize the area between them, it plugs into a power outlet or generator, and it leaves no arc marks. A yoke checked for lifting power meets the requirement in ASME Section V Article 7: at least ten pounds for an AC yoke and forty pounds for a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at the pole spacing used.

  • Visible particles: dry powder or a wet suspension in contrasting color, usually over a thin white paint background, practical on open structures.
  • Fluorescent particles: examined under UV-A light in a darkened enclosure, chosen for tight cracks on critical welds and shop parts.
  • Field verification: a pie gauge or field indicator confirms that the field is adequate and aimed in the right direction.
  • Demagnetizing: carried out when residual magnetism would interfere with welding, machining, instruments or service.

The procedure follows ASTM E1444 and Section V; our notes on Article 7 requirements and the complete MT guide give a closer look.

Reading indications on structures and rides

A fatigue crack from a weld toe usually appears as a fine, continuous line of particles along the toe or radiating from a corner, held tightly to the surface. A crack in a lifting lug often runs from the hole edge or across the throat of the weld. Fuzzy, wide smears of particles can mean a subsurface source, a change in section or leakage at an unfinished edge, and technicians re-examine such areas after cleaning or re-magnetizing before calling them relevant.

Relevant and non-relevant indications both exist on real equipment. Sharp edges, welded brackets, earlier test marks and machined radii all hold particles. The judgment of a Level II technician, with the procedure and acceptance criteria in hand, is what separates a rejectable crack from a harmless artifact. For ride and entertainment structures, a report that records each indication with a sketch and photograph helps the owner's engineer decide what is done next and later confirm that a repaired weld is clean.

Codes and Florida requirements

  • ASME Section V Article 7: method requirements, including yoke lifting power, light levels and two-direction examination.
  • ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6: magnetic particle methods and acceptance for pressure vessel welds.
  • ASME B31.3 and B31.1: piping examination requirements and acceptance tables.
  • AWS D1.1 and D1.5: structural welding code for steel and the bridge welding code used on Florida DOT work, which recognize magnetic particle testing for surface cracks.
  • API 510, 570 and 653: in-service codes; the authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection and Atlantis supplies the examination data.

In Florida the Boiler Safety Section of the Bureau of Fire Prevention in the Division of State Fire Marshal administers Chapter 554 of the Florida Statutes and Rule 69A-51 for boilers. The Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services regulates amusement rides and sets annual metal-fatigue testing and affidavit requirements for many rides. Whoever may perform that testing is set by the department's rule, so check it with the agency before you book work for a ride.

Who performs the work

Atlantis has no office in Orlando, and crews are mobilized to your site from outside the city. Technicians work to Atlantis's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up the yoke, checks the field, applies particles and interprets indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. The founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. When your contract names a code, the procedure is written to it so that lifting power, light, field direction and demagnetization requirements are fixed before work begins.

What the magnetic particle report contains

  • Part or weld identification, material, location, surface condition and test temperature.
  • Procedure number and revision, code and edition, and acceptance criteria used.
  • Yoke or prod equipment details, lifting-power or field check, particle type and batch, and UV-A and ambient light readings for fluorescent work.
  • Technician name and qualification level, date and conditions of the test.
  • Each indication by position, orientation and length, with accept or reject, and a sketch or photo.
  • Notes on demagnetization, post-cleaning and areas not examined.

Rejected indications are passed to your representative as found so that repair and re-examination can be arranged without delay.

Planning a magnetic particle job in Orlando

  • Thunderstorms: afternoon storms stop outdoor work and soak wet-method suspensions, so exterior examinations are planned for mornings with a fallback plan.
  • Heat: steel on exposed roofs, platforms and pads can exceed the temperature limits of the particle carrier, and the work moves into shade or cooler hours.
  • Humidity: morning dew and sweating surfaces affect paint contrast and particle adhesion, so surfaces must be dry before testing.
  • Guest areas and venues: work near the public happens outside operating hours, with escorts, badges and safety briefings agreed in advance.
  • Darkness for fluorescent work: a portable enclosure is set up in the area to be examined, which has to be planned with power and access.

Tell us the welds, finishes, access and your out-of-service dates, and we plan mobilization around them rather than promising an arrival time at the outset.

Choosing between MT, PT and UT in Orlando

Pick magnetic particle inspection for surface cracks on carbon and low-alloy steel, because it is quick and sensitive. Pick penetrant testing for stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals. Pick ultrasonic testing for remaining wall and internal weld flaws. The MT versus PT comparison sets out when each fits, the MT service overview describes the method in general, and the Florida inspection services hub gathers the statewide offering.

Training your own magnetic particle technicians

A facility with its own welded equipment gains from a trained person who checks critical welds between our visits. Atlantis teaches MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 under SNT-TC-1A, and the magnetic particle training overview lists the topics. Your company certifies its own technicians through its written practice, which we can help you write through written practice development. For central Florida employer options see NDT training for Orlando employers.

faq.q: What does magnetic particle inspection find in Orlando structures and plants?
faq.a: It finds surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel. In Orlando that covers attraction steel, lifting lugs and rigging, structural welds on towers and venues, and support welds on energy plant equipment.

faq.q: Will MPI work on aluminum or stainless steel parts?
faq.a: No. Aluminum and austenitic stainless steel are not magnetic, so the particles gather at no leakage field. Liquid penetrant testing is the usual choice for surface cracks in those materials.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Orlando for MT work?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Orlando. Technicians are mobilized to your property or plant with portable yokes and materials, and they issue a written report for the agreed scope of work.

faq.q: Is magnetic particle testing accepted for amusement ride fatigue checks in Florida?
faq.a: Florida requires non-destructive testing for metal fatigue on many rides, and MT is a common surface method. Who may perform it is set by the department's rule, so confirm with the agency first.

faq.q: Why is the yoke lifting power checked?
faq.a: Lifting power shows that the yoke produces enough field for the test. ASME Section V Article 7 calls for at least ten pounds for an AC yoke and forty pounds for DC or permanent-magnet yokes.

faq.q: Can fluorescent MT be done outdoors in Orlando?
faq.a: Yes, with a darkened enclosure and a UV-A light of the required intensity. Planning for the enclosure, power and ambient light belongs in the job scope, especially in bright central-Florida sun.

faq.q: When is demagnetization required after magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: It is required when residual magnetism could interfere with welding, machining, instruments or later service. Your procedure and specification say when it applies and how the residual field is checked.

faq.q: Who certifies the technicians who carry out MT for Atlantis?
faq.a: Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer qualifies and certifies its own personnel. Atlantis technicians are qualified under that company written practice, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train my facility team in magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and Level 2 training aligned with SNT-TC-1A, and your company then certifies its own technicians through its written practice after the training and experience are complete.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Orlando, FL | Dye Penetrant
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection in Orlando, FL for stainless piping, aluminum parts, welds and castings at plants, venues and shops, mobilized to site. Get a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Orlando, Florida
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out liquid penetrant testing, also known as dye penetrant inspection, in Orlando, Florida. The method shows cracks, porosity and laps that break the surface of stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, carbon steel and other non-porous materials. Typical work covers stainless piping and tanks, aluminum fabrications, weld repairs, machined and cast parts, and equipment at central-Florida plants and venues. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Describe the parts through the PT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Orlando

Metal that cannot be magnetized, or flaws that must be seen exactly where they break the surface, call for penetrant testing. Orlando has plenty of both. Hospitality, food service, water treatment and aviation support lean on stainless steel and aluminum, and the simulation and electronics industries machine small, valuable parts where a surface crack matters.

  • Resort, hotel and kitchen systems: stainless steam, domestic hot water and process piping, pressure vessels, heat exchangers and welded fittings that run continuously in humid conditions.
  • Water and wastewater facilities: stainless and alloy piping welds, pump and valve bodies, tank repairs and welds on equipment that sits in chemically active water.
  • Aviation and ground support: aluminum structures, stainless fittings, tooling and fabricated stands around the airport area where a crack could shut equipment down.
  • Machined and precision parts: housings, brackets and fixtures made for the region's defense and simulation industries, where surface finish and crack-free metal are required before assembly.
  • Repair and fabrication shops: root and cap passes on alloy piping, castings and forgings received from suppliers, and weld repairs on carbon steel when magnetic methods are not practical.

If the part is plain carbon steel and a crack is the concern, magnetic particle testing in Orlando is often faster. Penetrant testing is the answer when the metal or the geometry rules magnetic methods out.

What penetrant testing finds and what it misses

A thin liquid, either visible red dye or fluorescent dye, is applied to a clean dry surface and left to be drawn into any opening by capillary action. Excess is removed, a developer is applied, and the trapped liquid is pulled back out so that the flaw appears as a visible line or dot.

  • It finds: fatigue cracks, shrinkage cracks, laps, cold shuts, porosity and lack of fusion at the toe, provided the flaw is open to the surface.
  • It misses: subsurface flaws, defects plugged with oil, paint, or metal smeared by grinding or blasting, and anything on a very rough or porous surface where the liquid spreads everywhere.
  • It depends on cleaning: preparation carries more weight than any other step, since a sealed crack gives a clean-looking result that proves nothing.
  • It does not give depth: an indication shows length and position but not how deep the crack goes.

When depth or internal flaws matter, a follow-up with ultrasonic testing in Orlando sizes what the penetrant has found.

The sequence for a sound penetrant examination

  1. Pre-clean the area with solvent or cleaner to strip oil, grease, paint and scale, and allow it to dry completely.
  2. Apply the penetrant by spray, brush or immersion, using a visible Type II or a fluorescent Type I system, with a removal method chosen to suit the job: water-washable, post-emulsifiable or solvent-removable.
  3. Hold the dwell time stated in the procedure, which varies with the material, the flaw type and the temperature.
  4. Remove excess penetrant without washing it out of any flaw, avoiding over-removal.
  5. Apply developer in a thin, even coat and watch the indications bleed out, then evaluate within the development window.
  6. Post-clean so that residue does not interfere with later welding, coating or service.

Field crews often use solvent-removable visible dye, because it is portable and needs no water supply. The requirements are set out in the Article 6 guide.

Codes and Florida requirements

  • ASME Section V Article 6: liquid penetrant examination requirements, including materials control, temperature, dwell and developer.
  • ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8: penetrant methods and acceptance criteria for pressure vessels.
  • ASME B31.3 and B31.1: piping examination requirements and acceptance tables.
  • ASTM E165: the general-industry practice for penetrant testing.
  • AWS D1.1 and D1.6: structural and stainless steel welding codes, in which penetrant testing is recognized for surface examination of welds.
  • API 510 and 570: in-service codes, where the owner's authorized inspector holds responsibility and Atlantis reports each indication.

In Florida the Boiler Safety Section of the Bureau of Fire Prevention, in the Division of State Fire Marshal, administers Chapter 554 of the Florida Statutes and Rule 69A-51 for boilers, and the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services regulates amusement rides, including a requirement for periodic non-destructive testing for metal fatigue on many of them. Penetrant results can support those regimes, but the agency's rule decides who may perform testing on a ride, so confirm it before booking.

Who carries out penetrant examinations

Orlando has no Atlantis office, and technicians are mobilized from elsewhere to your site for the agreed scope. They work under Atlantis's written practice, which is based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician controls the materials, performs the examination and interprets the indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. The founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Penetrant materials are used as a matched family and batch-recorded, since mixing makers can ruin sensitivity.

What the penetrant report contains

  • Part or weld identification, material, finish and test temperature.
  • Procedure and revision, code and edition, and acceptance criteria applied.
  • Penetrant, remover and developer types with manufacturer and batch numbers, and the removal method used.
  • Dwell time, light conditions or UV-A intensity, and technician name and level.
  • Each indication by position, form (linear or rounded), size and accept or reject decision, with a sketch or photograph.
  • Notes on post-cleaning and any area that could not be examined.

Clear sketches help the repair crew find the same spot and let a later examiner compare the result.

Indications and how they are judged

On developer, a crack shows as a continuous or broken line, a cluster of porosity as scattered dots, and a lap or cold shut as a short curved mark. Indications grow as penetrant bleeds out, so the technician evaluates them within the development window set in the procedure, not at their largest. Machined threads, weld ripples, press fits and cleaning residue can look like flaws, and the technician wipes, re-develops or re-cleans to decide which are real.

Where a surface was ground, blasted or peened, metal may have been smeared over a crack, and etching followed by re-testing is used before accepting a clean result. Acceptance comes from the governing code: most codes reject linear indications beyond a stated length and evaluate rounded indications by size and spacing, and the report states the criterion applied so that the repair decision rests on a named rule.

Planning a penetrant job in Orlando

  • Temperature: the usual standard range is about 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for both part and materials, and hot roofs, pads and equipment in the Orlando sun can exceed it, so work shifts to shade or morning hours or uses a qualified procedure.
  • Humidity and dew: moisture left on a surface blocks penetrant, so cleaning and drying time carries extra weight in humid central Florida.
  • Storms: developer washes off and sprays drift in wind, and afternoon storms stop outdoor work, so exterior examinations are scheduled early.
  • Material limits: stainless and nickel alloys often require materials low in halogens and sulfur, and the plan should confirm this before materials are bought.
  • Public spaces: work in or near guest areas follows operating hours, escort rules and strict housekeeping, because solvent and developer must be controlled.

Send the materials, finish and out-of-service dates when you ask for a quote. We plan mobilization around them and do not promise a crew arrival time in advance.

Choosing between PT, MT and UT in Orlando

Choose liquid penetrant testing for surface cracks on stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals, and where particles cannot be applied. Choose magnetic particle testing for carbon and low-alloy steel when speed matters. Choose ultrasonic testing for wall thickness and internal weld flaws. The MT and PT comparison explains the trade-offs, the penetrant testing service overview covers the method, and the Florida inspection services hub collects the statewide offering.

Training your own penetrant technicians

A facility that welds stainless or aluminum often benefits from a trained penetrant technician on staff. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 training under SNT-TC-1A, with a PT practical simulator for practice, and the penetrant testing training overview lists the subjects. Your company certifies its own technicians through its written practice. See NDT training for Orlando employers for central Florida options.

faq.q: What does liquid penetrant testing find in Orlando equipment?
faq.a: It finds cracks, laps, porosity and other flaws open to the surface. In Orlando it is used on stainless piping, aluminum fabrications, weld repairs, castings and non-magnetic parts that magnetic particle testing cannot inspect.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing detect a crack below the surface?
faq.a: No. The liquid enters only flaws that break the surface. A buried crack or internal lack of fusion needs ultrasonic examination, which looks inside the section and estimates where the flaw sits.

faq.q: Why does cleaning matter so much for dye penetrant inspection?
faq.a: Grinding, blasting or paint can seal a crack so penetrant cannot enter. Careful cleaning and sometimes etching remove that cover, which is why many missed indications trace back to preparation rather than the dye.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Orlando for PT?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Orlando. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, venue or shop with portable materials, and they issue a written report listing each indication and its accept or reject result.

faq.q: What temperature range does penetrant testing allow?
faq.a: The usual standard range for the part and materials is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside it the procedure must be qualified for the temperature, which matters for hot surfaces in direct Orlando sun.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be used on stainless steel at resorts and kitchens?
faq.a: Yes, using materials with controlled halogen and sulfur content and cleaning them off afterward. The procedure states those limits, and residue removal protects equipment and later welding.

faq.q: Does Florida require nondestructive testing of amusement rides?
faq.a: Florida requires non-destructive testing for metal fatigue on many rides at least annually, by a technician meeting the department's rule. Check eligibility with the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services before booking.

faq.q: Who is responsible when Atlantis performs PT under API 510 or 570?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector holds responsibility for the inspection and repair decisions. Atlantis performs the penetrant examination and provides documented indications for that inspector to evaluate.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train my team in liquid penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 and Level 2 training aligned with ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and your company then qualifies and certifies its technicians through its own written practice after the requirements are met.
